data.title: Credential Extraction from Compromised Hosts
data.summary: Administrative access to compromised hosts was used to extract password hashes, Kerberos tickets, and cached credentials from the operating system, enabling further lateral movement and privilege escalation.
data.description:
When an attacker gains administrative access to a Windows host, several sources of credential material become accessible.

The LSASS process holds NTLM password hashes and Kerberos tickets for every user with an active or recent interactive session. Extracting this data yields the authentication material needed to impersonate those users on other systems.

The local Security Account Manager (SAM) database stores NTLM hashes for all local accounts. These hashes can be used for pass-the-hash attacks, and where local administrator passwords are shared across hosts, a single extraction compromises the entire group.

The DPAPI master keys on each host protect saved credentials in Windows Credential Manager, browser passwords stored by Chrome and Edge, and certificate private keys. With administrative access, these keys can be decrypted and the protected secrets recovered.

On domain controllers, the NTDS.dit database contains the NTLM hash and Kerberos keys for every account in the domain. Access to this file, whether through volume shadow copy or the DCSync technique, is equivalent to compromise of every domain account.

Credential material was extracted during this assessment from multiple hosts. The recovered hashes and tickets were used to authenticate to additional systems and escalate privileges within the domain.
data.impact: Each compromised host yielded credentials for accounts that had authenticated to it, including in several cases domain administrative accounts. This created a cascading chain where each new host provided access to further systems. The credentials recovered included those of service accounts, administrative users, and in one case the domain administrator, leading to full domain compromise.
data.recommendation:
1. Enable Credential Guard on all supported systems to isolate LSASS process memory, preventing extraction of NTLM hashes and Kerberos tickets by tools running as administrator.

2. Implement a tiered administration model so that privileged accounts authenticate only to systems of equivalent sensitivity. A domain administrator account should never log on to a workstation.

3. Configure the "Interactive logon: Number of previous logons to cache" policy to the minimum value the business requires, reducing the window during which cached credentials remain on disk.

4. Deploy Windows LAPS to assign unique local administrator passwords per host, so that extraction of the SAM database on one host does not grant access to others.

5. Monitor for access to the LSASS process by unexpected executables, and for volume shadow copy creation on domain controllers outside maintenance windows.

6. Restrict debug privileges (SeDebugPrivilege) through Group Policy to prevent non-administrative processes from reading LSASS memory.
